title: Transformations & Symmetry
coreInsight: Transformations reveal what changes and what remains invariant; rigid motions preserve distance and angle, while dilation changes scale in a controlled way.
targetLearnerRealization: Translation, rotation, and reflection move a figure without changing lengths or angles; reflection reverses orientation, dilation changes scale, and symmetry requires an exact self-match.
learningObjectives: Distinguish translation, rotation, reflection, and dilation by their defining actions.
Identify distance and angle invariants of rigid motions.
Track orientation under rotation versus reflection.
Test a proposed symmetry by exact point correspondence.
Apply coordinate rules and compose transformations.

continuity.openingCallback: Treat a rotation as a measured turn of an entire figure while preserving the angle relationships inside it.
closingSeeds: Mental rotation and reflection can predict which faces meet when a two-dimensional net folds into a solid.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Rotated or reflected copies count as different shapes.
A line of symmetry can be guessed by appearance without testing correspondence.
Reflection and rotation preserve orientation in the same way.

beats.purpose: Establish transformation invariants by comparing several moved copies of one scalene triangle.
beats.expectedRealization: Translation, rotation, and reflection preserve all side lengths and angle measures despite changed position or pose.
beats.transitionIn: A ray's rotation changed direction while its angle magnitude remained precise. Now move an entire triangle and track what survives.
beats.whyNow: A scalene figure prevents symmetry or prototype cues from hiding the invariant idea.
beats.entryBridge: Compare corresponding distances and angles, not screen position.
beats.exitBridge: All three rigid motions keep the 3-4-5 side lengths and all angle measures.
learnerPrompts: Which properties must every translated, rotated, or reflected copy preserve?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Side lengths and angle measures remain unchanged.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Position and facing may change; measure the internal distances and angles.

visual.ariaLabel: A triangle under rigid motions with lengths angles area and perimeter preserved

steps.body: A rigid motion moves every point without stretching, so distances and angles—and therefore area and perimeter—are preserved.

resolution.takeaway: A moved copy is the same size and shape even when it looks unfamiliar.

beats.purpose: Distinguish reflection from rotation through vertex order.
beats.expectedRealization: Translation and rotation preserve clockwise order; reflection reverses it.
beats.transitionIn: Lengths and angles cannot distinguish the three rigid motions. Track the order of labeled vertices instead.
beats.prompt: Vertices A, B, C appear clockwise on a triangle. After which single transformation must their image order become counterclockwise?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. A mirror reverses orientation; sliding and turning do not.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Imagine written letters on transparent paper: only flipping the paper reverses clockwise order.

steps.body: Rotation changes facing but preserves vertex order. Reflection crosses a mirror line and reverses clockwise/counterclockwise orientation.

resolution.takeaway: Reflection preserves lengths and angles but reverses orientation.

beats.purpose: Separate dilation from rigid motions using scale.
beats.expectedRealization: A dilation preserves angles and proportional shape but multiplies all distances by k.
beats.transitionIn: Now move each point away from a center by twice its original distance.
beats.prompt: A dilation has scale factor 2. Which statement is true?

options.text: Angles stay equal, but every length doubles.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Dilation changes size in a controlled way and is not rigid unless k=1.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A scale factor acts on distances from the center and corresponding lengths, not angle measures.

steps.body: Length factor is 2, perimeter factor 2, and area factor 4. Equal angles keep the figure similar, not congruent.

resolution.takeaway: Dilation preserves shape but generally changes size.

beats.purpose: Define line symmetry through exact reflection rather than visual guessing.
beats.expectedRealization: A line is a symmetry axis only if every point's reflection lands on the figure.
beats.transitionIn: A reflection can also leave an entire figure occupying the same set of points.
beats.prompt: What test proves that a proposed line is a line of symmetry?

options.text: Reflect every point across it and check the image coincides with the figure.
Check that the line splits the picture into equal areas only.
Check that it passes through the center.
Judge whether the halves look similar.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Symmetry requires point-for-point coincidence after reflection.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Equal area or a central line is not enough; corresponding points must land exactly.

steps.body: A fold is a useful physical model: every point on one side must meet its mirror point on the other, while points on the axis stay fixed.

resolution.takeaway: Symmetry is an exact transformation test, not an appearance judgment.

beats.purpose: Name transformation types and invariants after learners have compared their effects.
beats.expectedRealization: The operation determines which properties are invariant.
beats.name: Transformations and symmetry
beats.conciseDefinition: A translation slides, a rotation turns about a center, a reflection flips across a line, and a dilation scales from a center. The first three are rigid motions; symmetry means a transformation maps a figure onto itself.
beats.formalization: rigid: distance and angle preserved · reflection reverses orientation · dilation length factor k, area factor k²
beats.memoryHook: Slide, turn, flip: rigid. Scale: similar. Self-match: symmetry.

beats.purpose: Apply exact reflection tests across familiar polygon families.
beats.expectedRealization: The square has four valid reflection axes; tempting diagonals fail for a non-square rectangle.
beats.transitionIn: Place the mirror line over each figure and count only axes whose reflection matches every point.
beats.whyNow: The learner has a point-correspondence definition, so the contest comparison can repair diagonal and appearance traps.
beats.entryBridge: Test each candidate axis by folding, including the rectangle's diagonals.
beats.exitBridge: Counts 3,2,2,1,4 make the square the unique maximum.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A reflection axis overlaid on a figure and tested point by point.
learnerPrompts: How many axes work for the equilateral triangle?
Which diagonals work for the rhombus?
Why do a non-square rectangle's diagonals fail?
What single axis works for the isosceles trapezoid?
Which four axes work for the square?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The square has the greatest count, with four lines of symmetry.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Fold each figure across every candidate line and count only exact self-matches.

steps.title: Test every figure
steps.body: The counts are 3 for the equilateral triangle, 2 for the non-square rhombus, 2 for the non-square rectangle, 1 for the isosceles trapezoid, and 4 for the square.

steps.title: Reject the rectangle trap
steps.body: A non-square rectangle's diagonal swaps unequal side directions, so its halves do not coincide.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Four is the greatest count, so the square wins.

resolution.takeaway: A candidate symmetry line must pass the reflection test for the whole figure.

beats.purpose: Construct missing reflected partners instead of merely recognizing symmetry.
beats.expectedRealization: Reflecting cell coordinates across diagonal BD pairs four unmatched black squares with four required additions.
beats.transitionIn: The last task tested complete shapes. Now repair an incomplete grid so one specified diagonal becomes an exact mirror.
beats.whyNow: The learner can track point correspondence and is ready to minimize additions by filling only missing partners.
beats.entryBridge: Reflect every existing black cell, ignore self-matched cells on the axis, and count distinct missing partners.
beats.exitBridge: Exactly four reflected cells are absent, so four additions are necessary and sufficient.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A mirror line mapping discrete cells to partner cells.
learnerPrompts: How does diagonal BD map a row-column cell to its partner?
Why are four additions both sufficient and minimal?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Four distinct reflected partners must be added.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Reflect each black cell across BD; count only partner cells that are not already black and not on the axis.

steps.title: Apply the mirror map
steps.body: Each black cell must have a black partner at equal perpendicular distance across BD.

steps.title: Count missing images
steps.body: Four existing cells map to four distinct uncolored partners.

steps.title: Prove minimality
steps.body: Every missing partner is necessary, and adding those four makes every pair match, so the minimum is 4.

resolution.takeaway: To complete symmetry, add every distinct missing image and no others.

beats.whyNow: Return to a single operation after the symmetry constructions.
beats.entryBridge: Apply the same displacement vector to both coordinates.
learnerPrompts: What horizontal and vertical changes act on every point?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Add 4 to x and subtract 3 from y.

resolution.takeaway: A translation adds one common vector to every point.

beats.whyNow: Use G1's 90-degree turn in the coordinate plane.
beats.entryBridge: Turn the vector from the origin counterclockwise.
learnerPrompts: Where do the positive x and positive y directions turn?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. A 90° counterclockwise rotation sends (3,1) to (−1,3).
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use (x,y)→(−y,x) for a quarter-turn counterclockwise about the origin.

steps.body: (3,1)→(−1,3). Distance from the origin remains sqrt(10).

resolution.takeaway: Rotation changes direction while preserving distance.

beats.purpose: Assess coordinate reflection and orientation reversal.
beats.whyNow: Contrast the quarter-turn with a mirror rule.
beats.entryBridge: Keep height and reverse horizontal position across the y-axis.
learnerPrompts: Which signed distance from the mirror changes?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Across the y-axis, x changes sign and y stays fixed.

resolution.takeaway: Reflection reverses perpendicular distance across its mirror line.

beats.purpose: Assess dilation's non-rigid length and area changes.
beats.whyNow: Separate similarity from rigid congruence numerically.
beats.entryBridge: Multiply lengths by k and area by k².
beats.exitBridge: k=3 doubles no distances; perimeter triples and area multiplies by 9.
learnerPrompts: Which measures prove the motion is not rigid?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Perimeter is 36 and area is 90.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use one factor 3 on perimeter and 3² on area.

steps.body: P=12×3=36; A=10×9=90. Changed lengths show the dilation is not rigid.

resolution.takeaway: Dilation preserves angles, not absolute distances.

beats.purpose: Assess order-sensitive composition of rigid motions.
beats.whyNow: Finish by coordinating two transformation rules.
beats.entryBridge: Apply the stated first operation before the second.
beats.exitBridge: Translation gives (3,4), then y-axis reflection gives (−3,4).
learnerPrompts: What is the intermediate image before reflection?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Translate (1,2) by (2,2) first, then reflect the result across the y-axis.

steps.body: (1,2)→(3,4)→(−3,4). Reversing the operation order would generally differ.

resolution.takeaway: Transformation composition follows the written order.

beats.purpose: Consolidate operation, invariant, orientation, and symmetry checks.
beats.expectedRealization: A transformation is understood by its point rule and preserved quantities.
beats.transitionIn: Triangles, coordinates, mirror grids, and scaled figures all changed some features while protecting others.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable transformation routine? Select all four.

options.text: Identify the point rule or center/axis/vector.
Track lengths and angles to test rigidity.
Check whether clockwise order is preserved or reversed.
Require exact coincidence when testing self-symmetry.

response.feedback: Each action distinguishes transformations that may look similar.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Define the motion, track invariants and orientation, then test exact correspondence.

steps.body: The name of a motion is shorthand for a point mapping. Its invariant and orientation behavior provide independent checks.

resolution.takeaway: Follow points, then read what changed and what survived.

beats.purpose: Create the approved bridge from plane transformations to cube-net reasoning.
beats.expectedRealization: Folding a net requires mentally rotating faces rigidly around shared edges and tracking adjacency.
beats.transitionIn: A reflection repaired a flat grid by pairing cells. A fold moves flat faces into space without stretching them.
beats.prompt: When a cube net folds, which rigid motions help predict where each face lands and which faces become opposite?
beats.takeaway: Mental rotation preserves face shape and edge length while changing orientation and adjacency in space.

notes: Design: a scalene triangle moved by three rigid motions reveals distance/angle invariants. Vertex order distinguishes reflection, dilation contrasts with rigidity, and exact self-reflection defines line symmetry. Authentic problems test candidate axes and construct missing mirror partners.

Beat outline: rigid-copy anchor -> orientation -> dilation contrast -> exact fold test -> name -> authentic shape comparison -> authentic grid repair -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> cube-net hook.
Both mapped animations are referenced unchanged after submission over their full timelines. Existing generic choice-grid visuals suffice; no renderer or animation source changes were made.
Generated results were verified with coordinate rules, distance checks, dimensional scale factors, and independent inverse or operation-order audits. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
